entities.summary:
Theism, the belief in the existence of at least one deity, stands as one of humanity's most enduring and globally pervasive intellectual constructs, fundamentally shaping civilizations across all continents and eras. From the earliest organized cults of the Neolithic Revolution (c. 10,000 BCE) through the Axial Age (c. 800-200 BCE) and into the modern era, theistic frameworks have provided comprehensive explanations for the cosmos, human existence, ethics, and social order. Its significance lies in its capacity to inspire monumental cultural achievements, justify political authority, and mobilize populations for both collective good and conflict, making it a central force in the historical development of nearly every society.

Historically, theism manifested in diverse forms, ranging from the complex polytheistic pantheons of ancient Mesopotamia and Egypt, where deities like Enlil and Ra governed cosmic and earthly affairs, to the emergent monotheistic traditions of Judaism (c. 2000 BCE), Zoroastrianism (c. 6th century BCE), and later Christianity (1st century CE) and Islam (7th century CE). These systems often codified beliefs into sacred texts—such as the Rigveda (c. 1500-1200 BCE) in India or the Torah in the Levant—establishing ritual practices, moral codes, and clerical hierarchies. Theistic beliefs spurred the construction of vast temples, cathedrals, and mosques, served as the bedrock for legal systems like Hammurabi's Code (c. 1754 BCE), and fueled philosophical inquiries into the nature of reality and the divine.
